by_task.when: Arizona exemptions are allowable and the asset is being classified under a capped personal-property or homestead provision.
by_task.procedure: Decide eligibility from the asset category, not whether its value is below the cap. Under the independent-pair task, test each motor vehicle under Ariz. Rev. Stat. § 33-1125(8) and each firearm under § 33-1125(10). Use § 33-1125(1) only for wearing apparel, and use § 33-1101(A) for a qualifying occupied residence; subsection (B) states the homestead limit rather than a separate asset exemption. Section 33-1125(4) covers only engagement and wedding rings, not other jewelry; output only § 33-1101(A), not subsection (B), for the homestead alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reject an eligible firearm or vehicle solely because its value exceeds the dollar limit, do not treat jewelry as wearing apparel, and do not list § 33-1101(B) as another homestead alternative.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are an allowable namespace and the asset is property of the estate.
by_task.procedure: Test 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) independently for every asset because it covers any property; include it in addition to every applicable specific federal exemption. Classify the specific exemption by the statutory category: § 522(d)(4) is jewelry, and § 522(d)(3) is limited to its enumerated household categories. Add § 522(d)(5) before testing specifics; also test a motor vehicle under § 522(d)(2) regardless of value and a professionally prescribed health aid under § 522(d)(9).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use federal exemptions when the supplied allowable jurisdictions exclude them, and do not label a firearm as household goods or jewelry merely because it is personally owned.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for each independently considered asset-exemption pair.
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(5) as a separate alternative for every asset and report the lesser of the asset value and $15,425 per debtor: $1,475 plus the full $13,950 unused-homestead amount available in this independent-pair task. For two joint debtors, the combined ceiling is $30,850 under § 522(m). Apply each specific federal cap separately, including $700 per item under § 522(d)(3). For jointly owned property of two debtors, compare the asset value directly with $30,850, not $15,425. Treat each separately listed asset as one item for the $700 limit even if its description denotes a pair or set.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reduce the wildcard by allocations to other assets, do not omit it because a specific exemption also applies, and do not use a specific category that the asset does not satisfy.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal rather than business property.
by_task.procedure: Test 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for every personal-property asset and include it independently alongside any applicable specific exemption, including wearing apparel under (a), a motor vehicle under (c), or a professionally prescribed health aid under (e).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit (b) merely because a specific subsection applies; do not use the personal-property exemptions for business-use property, and do not classify an ordinary household appliance as a tool of trade without facts showing trade use.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and claim values must be reported independently.
by_task.procedure: Under § 5/12-1001(b), report the lesser of value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for two joint debtors. Separately cap a motor-vehicle alternative under (c) at $2,400; wearing apparel under (a) and professionally prescribed health aids under (e) protect the asset value because the supplied text states no dollar cap. Begin every personal-use asset with its independent (b) alternative, then add any applicable specific subsection; apply (a) only to actual clothing, not jewelry or watches.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 wildcard limit for the $2,400 motor-vehicle limit, do not double the motor-vehicle limit, and do not omit an uncapped specific alternative merely because (b) also applies.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative in addition to any applicable Oregon category exemption and any allowable federal exemption. List (p) for each personal-property asset before testing categories; a musical instrument uses § 18.345(1)(a), a motor vehicle uses (d), and a professionally prescribed health aid uses (h). A value above a category cap limits the EV amount but does not defeat EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 18.345(1)(p) because the asset already qualifies as clothing, jewelry, household goods, a vehicle, an animal, a health aid, or another specific category; do not apply it to real property.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property requiring an independent claim value.
by_task.procedure: For Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p), report the lesser of the asset value and $400 as a separate alternative, while calculating each specific Oregon exemption under its own limit. If the asset value is below $400, report that value rather than $400.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the asset's full value when it exceeds $400, and do not consume or suppress this alternative because another exemption is also listed.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative for every kind of property, even when a federal or a particular Pennsylvania exemption also applies. Apply § 8124(a)(1) only to actual wearing apparel. Start each asset with § 8123, then add any applicable specific alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because the asset lacks a matching § 8124 category, and do not treat a firearm or other nonclothing item as wearing apparel.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and an independent claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: For § 8123 report the lesser of the asset value and $300 for one debtor; because each spouse is entitled to it, use a combined ceiling of $600 for jointly owned property of two debtors. Preserve any separately applicable federal or Pennsylvania alternative. Determine the debtor count from the facts: never use $600 for a single debtor, and never report more than the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not allocate the monetary exemption across assets in this independent-pair task or replace a specific exemption with § 8123.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and an asset qualifies as consumer goods under Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(d).
by_task.procedure: Report the lesser of the asset value and the applicable § 815.18(3)(d) ceiling. The $12,000 single-debtor limit is a ceiling, not the claim value; if the consumer good is worth less, report its actual value. Section 815.18(8) may combine spouses' ceilings, but the claim still cannot exceed the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not automatically report $12,000 for every eligible consumer good, and do not use subsection (d) for property whose facts instead establish business use, a motor vehicle, a depository account or real property.

Use § 33-1125(1) only for wearing apparel, and use § 33-1101(A) for a qualifying occupied residence; subsection (B) states the homestead limit rather than a separate asset exemption. Section 33-1125(4) covers only engagement and wedding rings, not other jewelry; output only § 33-1101(A), not subsection (B), for the homestead alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reject an eligible firearm or vehicle solely because its value exceeds the dollar limit, do not treat jewelry as wearing apparel, and do not list § 33-1101(B) as another homestead alternative.

operations.rationale: The current Arizona EC parent still listed subsection (B) as a separate homestead exemption and treated non-ring jewelry as an engagement-or-wedding-ring exemption. The added category boundaries address those false positives while preserving the already successful cap-as-amount rule.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are an allowable namespace and the asset is property of the estate.
by_task.procedure: Test 11 U.S.C. § 522(d)(5) independently for every asset because it covers any property; include it in addition to every applicable specific federal exemption. Classify the specific exemption by the statutory category: § 522(d)(4) is jewelry, and § 522(d)(3) is limited to its enumerated household categories. Add § 522(d)(5) before testing specifics; also test a motor vehicle under § 522(d)(2) regardless of value and a professionally prescribed health aid under § 522(d)(9).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use federal exemptions when the supplied allowable jurisdictions exclude them, and do not label a firearm as household goods or jewelry merely because it is personally owned.

by_task.when: Federal exemptions are allowable and a claim value is required for each independently considered asset-exemption pair.
by_task.procedure: Include § 522(d)(5) as a separate alternative for every asset and report the lesser of the asset value and $15,425 per debtor: $1,475 plus the full $13,950 unused-homestead amount available in this independent-pair task. For two joint debtors, the combined ceiling is $30,850 under § 522(m). Apply each specific federal cap separately, including $700 per item under § 522(d)(3). For jointly owned property of two debtors, compare the asset value directly with $30,850, not $15,425. Treat each separately listed asset as one item for the $700 limit even if its description denotes a pair or set.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not reduce the wildcard by allocations to other assets, do not omit it because a specific exemption also applies, and do not use a specific category that the asset does not satisfy.

operations.rationale: The current parent continued to omit the federal wildcard when a specific exemption existed, excluded an over-cap vehicle at EC, omitted specific appliance or health-aid alternatives, used the single-debtor wildcard ceiling for joint debtors, and doubled the per-item household limit for a paired asset.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal rather than business property.
by_task.procedure: Test 735 Ill. Comp. Stat. 5/12-1001(b) for every personal-property asset and include it independently alongside any applicable specific exemption, including wearing apparel under (a), a motor vehicle under (c), or a professionally prescribed health aid under (e).
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit (b) merely because a specific subsection applies; do not use the personal-property exemptions for business-use property, and do not classify an ordinary household appliance as a tool of trade without facts showing trade use.

by_task.when: Illinois exemptions are allowable and claim values must be reported independently.
by_task.procedure: Under § 5/12-1001(b), report the lesser of value and $4,000 for one debtor or $8,000 for two joint debtors. Separately cap a motor-vehicle alternative under (c) at $2,400; wearing apparel under (a) and professionally prescribed health aids under (e) protect the asset value because the supplied text states no dollar cap. Begin every personal-use asset with its independent (b) alternative, then add any applicable specific subsection; apply (a) only to actual clothing, not jewelry or watches.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not substitute the $4,000 wildcard limit for the $2,400 motor-vehicle limit, do not double the motor-vehicle limit, and do not omit an uncapped specific alternative merely because (b) also applies.

operations.rationale: Illinois EC guidance remains verbatim because its current coordinate is already correct. The EV parent still omitted subsection (b) beside apparel, vehicles and health aids, omitted it for other personal assets, and mislabeled jewelry as wearing apparel; the EV-only addition targets those unresolved errors.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property.
by_task.procedure: Include Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p) as an independent alternative in addition to any applicable Oregon category exemption and any allowable federal exemption. List (p) for each personal-property asset before testing categories; a musical instrument uses § 18.345(1)(a), a motor vehicle uses (d), and a professionally prescribed health aid uses (h). A value above a category cap limits the EV amount but does not defeat EC eligibility.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 18.345(1)(p) because the asset already qualifies as clothing, jewelry, household goods, a vehicle, an animal, a health aid, or another specific category; do not apply it to real property.

by_task.when: Oregon exemptions are allowable and the asset is personal property requiring an independent claim value.
by_task.procedure: For Or. Rev. Stat. § 18.345(1)(p), report the lesser of the asset value and $400 as a separate alternative, while calculating each specific Oregon exemption under its own limit. If the asset value is below $400, report that value rather than $400.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not use the asset's full value when it exceeds $400, and do not consume or suppress this alternative because another exemption is also listed.

operations.rationale: The current parent repeatedly omitted subsection (p), misclassified a musical instrument, excluded an over-cap vehicle at EC, and sometimes reported $400 for property worth less than $400. The update distinguishes missing alternatives, category selection and amount calculation.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and the asset is property of the judgment debtor.
by_task.procedure: Include 42 Pa. Cons. Stat. § 8123 as an independent alternative for every kind of property, even when a federal or a particular Pennsylvania exemption also applies. Apply § 8124(a)(1) only to actual wearing apparel. Start each asset with § 8123, then add any applicable specific alternative.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not omit § 8123 because the asset lacks a matching § 8124 category, and do not treat a firearm or other nonclothing item as wearing apparel.

by_task.when: Pennsylvania exemptions are allowable and an independent claim value is required.
by_task.procedure: For § 8123 report the lesser of the asset value and $300 for one debtor; because each spouse is entitled to it, use a combined ceiling of $600 for jointly owned property of two debtors. Preserve any separately applicable federal or Pennsylvania alternative. Determine the debtor count from the facts: never use $600 for a single debtor, and never report more than the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not allocate the monetary exemption across assets in this independent-pair task or replace a specific exemption with § 8123.

operations.rationale: The parent still omitted § 8123 from several assets, falsely treated nonclothing property as wearing apparel, and used the two-debtor $600 ceiling in a single-debtor case even when it exceeded the asset value.

by_task.when: Wisconsin exemptions are allowable and an asset qualifies as consumer goods under Wis. Stat. § 815.18(3)(d).
by_task.procedure: Report the lesser of the asset value and the applicable § 815.18(3)(d) ceiling. The $12,000 single-debtor limit is a ceiling, not the claim value; if the consumer good is worth less, report its actual value. Section 815.18(8) may combine spouses' ceilings, but the claim still cannot exceed the asset value.
by_task.avoid_when: Do not automatically report $12,000 for every eligible consumer good, and do not use subsection (d) for property whose facts instead establish business use, a motor vehicle, a depository account or real property.

operations.rationale: For every Wisconsin consumer good in the witnessed EV failure, the parent output the $12,000 statutory ceiling instead of the lesser asset value. This is a distinct amount correction not supplied by the federal wildcard skill.
